heading: Duty to have fall protection.
title: Fall protection inspection (29 CFR 1926.501)
description: Fall protection inspection under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.501: requirements by paragraph, FY2022–FY2026 citation data and a printable site checklist.
opening: 29 CFR 1926.501 requires employers to confirm that walking/working surfaces can support workers safely and to protect each employee 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level with guardrail, safety net or personal fall arrest systems, or another measure the section allows.

enforcementSummary: Paragraph 1926.501(b)(13), which covers employees in residential construction activities at 6 feet or higher, is the most-cited paragraph for FY2022–FY2026. It is followed by (b)(1) on unprotected sides and edges, (b)(10) on roofing work on low-slope roofs and (b)(11) on steep roofs. Annual citations were 8,286 in FY2022, 9,189 in FY2023, 8,868 in FY2024, 9,080 in FY2025 and 6,503 in FY2026.
requirementsIntro: Section 1926.501 sets out when employers must provide fall protection systems, and every system it requires must meet the criteria in § 1926.502. Paragraph (a) covers general duties. Paragraphs (b)(1) to (b)(15) name work situations and the systems allowed in each, which are mostly guardrail, safety net or personal fall arrest systems (called conventional systems below). Paragraph (c) covers falling objects.

requirements.heading: What general duties does 1926.501(a) place on employers?
requirements.intro: Under 1926.501(a), employers must use fall protection that meets § 1926.502 and must confirm that a surface is strong enough before anyone works on it.

items.text: Any fall protection that this section requires must conform to the criteria in § 1926.502.
The employer must determine whether each walking/working surface has the strength and structural integrity to support employees safely. Employees may work on that surface only once it does.

requirements.heading: When must employers provide fall protection at edges, openings and hoist areas?
requirements.intro: Under 1926.501(b), edges, wall openings, walkways and hoist areas need protection once the drop to a lower level reaches 6 feet (1.8 m).

items.text: Each employee on a horizontal or vertical walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level must be protected by a conventional system.
On ramps, runways and other walkways, employees must be protected by guardrail systems from falls of 6 feet or more to lower levels.

Employees working on, at, above or near a wall opening, including one with a chute attached, need a conventional system when the opening's outside bottom edge is at least 6 feet above a lower level and its inside bottom edge is less than 39 inches (1.0 m) above the walking/working surface.
In hoist areas, employees must be protected from falls of 6 feet or more by guardrail or personal fall arrest systems.
If a guardrail, chain or gate is removed for hoisting and an employee must lean through the access opening or out over its edge, that employee must be protected by a personal fall arrest system.

Each employee on any other walking/working surface at a height of 6 feet or more needs a conventional system. The exceptions are surfaces covered by § 1926.500(a)(2) or by 1926.501(b)(1) through (b)(14).

requirements.heading: What protection is required at holes, excavations and dangerous equipment?
requirements.intro: Holes, excavations and dangerous equipment each have their own rule in 1926.501(b)(4), (b)(7) and (b)(8), and covers are named more often here than at open edges.

items.text: Employees must be protected from falling through holes, including skylights, that are more than 6 feet above lower levels. The allowed measures are personal fall arrest systems, covers, or guardrail systems erected around the hole.
Covers must protect employees from tripping in, or stepping into or through, holes and skylights.
Covers must also protect employees from objects falling through holes and skylights.
At the edge of an excavation at least 6 feet deep that cannot readily be seen because of plant growth or another visual barrier, employees need guardrail systems, fences or barricades.
At the edge of a well, pit, shaft or similar excavation with a depth of 6 feet or more, employees need guardrail systems, fences, barricades or covers.
Employees less than 6 feet above dangerous equipment must be protected from falling into or onto it by guardrail systems or equipment guards.
Employees 6 feet or higher above dangerous equipment need guardrail, personal fall arrest or safety net systems.

requirements.heading: What fall protection does 1926.501 require for roofing work?
requirements.intro: Roofing work with unprotected sides and edges at 6 feet (1.8 m) or higher is covered by 1926.501(b)(10) for low-slope roofs and by (b)(11) for steep roofs.

items.text: Unless another part of paragraph (b) provides otherwise, employees doing roofing work on low-slope roofs need either a conventional system or a warning line system combined with a guardrail system, safety net system, personal fall arrest system or safety monitoring system.
A safety monitoring system alone, without a warning line system, is permitted on low-slope roofs 50 feet (15.25 m) or less in width (see appendix A to subpart M).
On steep roofs, employees need guardrail systems with toeboards, safety net systems or personal fall arrest systems.

requirements.heading: When can a fall protection plan replace conventional systems?
requirements.intro: Section 1926.501 allows a fall protection plan that meets § 1926.502(k) for three kinds of work: leading edge work, precast concrete erection and residential construction. Each one applies only when the employer can demonstrate that conventional systems are infeasible or create a greater hazard.

items.text: Employees constructing a leading edge 6 feet or more above lower levels need a conventional system, subject to the fall protection plan exception.

Employees on the same elevated surface who are not doing the leading edge work also need a conventional system. If guardrails are chosen and a controlled access zone is already set up for the leading edge work, its control line may be used instead of a guardrail along the edge that runs parallel to the leading edge.

Employees erecting precast concrete members, such as wall panels, columns, beams, and floor and roof tees, or doing related work such as grouting at 6 feet or higher, need a conventional system. This applies unless another provision of paragraph (b) allows an alternative measure, and it is subject to the plan exception.

Employees doing residential construction activities 6 feet or more above lower levels need a conventional system. This applies unless another provision of paragraph (b) allows an alternative measure, and it is subject to the plan exception.

requirements.heading: What applies to formwork, reinforcing steel and overhand bricklaying?
requirements.intro: Formwork, reinforcing steel and overhand bricklaying each have their own lists of allowed systems in 1926.501(b)(5) and (b)(9).

items.text: Employees on the face of formwork or reinforcing steel must be protected from falls of 6 feet or more by personal fall arrest, safety net or positioning device systems.

Except where paragraph (b) provides otherwise, employees doing overhand bricklaying and related work at 6 feet or higher need a guardrail, safety net or personal fall arrest system, or must work in a controlled access zone.
An employee who reaches more than 10 inches (25 cm) below the level of the walking/working surface they are on needs a guardrail, safety net or personal fall arrest system.

requirements.heading: How must employers protect employees from falling objects?
requirements.intro: When an employee is exposed to falling objects, 1926.501(c) requires each employee to wear a hard hat and the employer to put one of three measures in place.

items.text: Each employee exposed to falling objects must wear a hard hat, and the employer must also use one of the measures in (c)(1) to (c)(3).
Option 1: erect toeboards, screens or guardrail systems that stop objects from falling from higher levels.
Option 2: erect a canopy structure and keep potential falling objects far enough back from the edge of the higher level that they would not go over if accidentally displaced.
Option 3: barricade the area where objects could fall, prohibit employees from entering it, and keep objects far enough back from the edge above that they would not go over if accidentally displaced.

checklistIntro: Supervisors can use this checklist to walk the site against each paragraph of 1926.501, which sets no inspection schedule of its own; we suggest using it before work at height starts and whenever edges, holes, roofs or hoist areas change.

faq.question: Who has to prove that guardrails, nets and fall arrest systems are infeasible?
faq.answer: The employer does. Notes to 1926.501(b)(2)(i), (b)(12) and (b)(13) say it is presumed that at least one of the listed systems is feasible and will not create a greater hazard. The employer therefore carries the burden of showing that a § 1926.502(k) plan is appropriate for the particular workplace situation.

faq.question: Does 1926.501 cover bricklaying done from scaffolds?
faq.answer: No. A note to 1926.501(b)(9)(ii) says that bricklaying operations performed on scaffolds are regulated by subpart L (Scaffolds) of Part 1926.
